title: Turn on two-step login for email
whatToDo: Require a code from a phone app every time someone signs in to company email from a new device.
why: Stolen email passwords are behind most payment fraud and many ransomware attacks. A phone code blocks almost all of these break-ins, even when the password is known.
steps: Sign in to your email provider's admin settings with an administrator account.
Find the security settings for two-step verification (also called multi-factor authentication or MFA) and turn it on for all users.
Ask each person to install an authenticator app (such as Microsoft Authenticator or Google Authenticator) and follow the setup prompt on their next sign-in.
Give people a one-week deadline, then make it required for everyone, including owners and managers.

m365: Go to entra.microsoft.com and sign in with your Microsoft 365 admin account.
Open Identity, then Overview, then Properties, and select 'Manage security defaults'. Set Security defaults to Enabled and save.
Tell staff that on their next sign-in they will be asked to install the Microsoft Authenticator app and scan a code. It takes about 5 minutes each.
Check the next day in the admin center (Users, then Active users, then Multi-factor authentication) that everyone has registered.
Keep one emergency 'break glass' admin account with a long password stored somewhere safe, in case a phone is lost.
google: Go to admin.google.com and sign in with your Google Workspace admin account.
Open Security, then Authentication, then 2-step verification. Check 'Allow users to turn on 2-step verification'.
Ask staff to turn it on at myaccount.google.com/security using the Google Authenticator app or a phone prompt.
After one week, return to the same admin page and set Enforcement to 'On' so it is required for everyone.
Keep backup codes for the admin account in a safe place, in case a phone is lost.

title: Turn on two-step login for banking, accounting, and portals
whatToDo: Switch on phone codes for online banking, accounting software, load boards, and fleet or TMS portals.
why: These are the accounts where money and loads move. Criminals who get in can redirect payments or steal loads, and a phone code stops most of them.
steps: Make a list of every online tool that touches money or loads: online banking, accounting (QuickBooks, Sage, Xero), load boards, fleet telematics, and TMS portals.
For each one, sign in and look under Security or Account settings for 'two-step', '2FA', or 'multi-factor'. Turn it on.
Use an authenticator app rather than text messages where the tool allows it.
For tools that do not offer it, ask the vendor when it is coming, and use a unique strong password in the meantime.
Tick each one off your list so you know nothing was missed.

title: Give everyone their own login and stop sharing accounts
whatToDo: Replace shared logins and shared tablets with a personal login for each person, protected with a PIN.
why: With shared accounts you cannot tell who did what, and you cannot cut off one person without disrupting everyone. Personal logins fix both.
steps: List every shared login in use: dispatch or load board accounts, shared email inboxes, shared tablets in trucks or on the floor.
Check whether each tool allows extra users. Many load boards and TMS tools include extra seats or charge a small amount per user.
Create a named account for each person, and use shared mailboxes (not shared passwords) for team inboxes.
Set a PIN on every work phone and tablet and turn on remote wipe through your email provider's device settings.
Change the old shared password once everyone has moved over, so it no longer works.

m365: Go to admin.microsoft.com and sign in with your Microsoft 365 admin account.
Under Users, then Active users, select 'Add a user' for each person who currently shares a login.
Create a shared mailbox instead of a shared password: go to Teams & groups, then Shared mailboxes, then 'Add a shared mailbox' for team inboxes.
Enroll phones and tablets in mobile device management (Devices, then Enrollment) to require a PIN and allow remote wipe.
Once everyone has moved over, change the old shared password so it no longer works.
google: Go to admin.google.com and sign in with your Google Workspace admin account.
Under Directory, then Users, select 'Add new user' for each person who currently shares a login.
Create a Google Group with a collaborative inbox instead of a shared password: go to Groups, then 'Create group', then turn on 'Collaborative Inbox' under access settings.
Enroll phones and tablets under Devices, then Mobile & endpoints, to require a PIN and allow remote wipe.
Once everyone has moved over, change the old shared password so it no longer works.

title: Create an offboarding checklist
whatToDo: Write a one-page checklist of every system and vendor with access, and use it the same day anyone leaves.
why: Forgotten accounts of former staff and old vendors are an easy way in. A checklist makes removing access fast and routine.
steps: Start a simple document or spreadsheet listing every system people log into: email, banking, accounting, load boards, telematics, door codes, and Wi-Fi.
Add every outside vendor or IT provider that can access your systems, with a contact name for each.
When someone leaves, go down the list that same day: disable accounts, collect devices, and change any shared passwords they knew.
Review the vendor list every six months and remove anyone you no longer work with.

m365: In your checklist, note that access is cut in admin.microsoft.com under Users, then Active users: select the person and choose 'Block sign-in'.
From the same page, reset their password and remove them from Microsoft 365 groups and Teams.
Add every outside vendor or IT provider with delegated admin access (Settings, then Partner relationships) to the list with a contact name.
When someone leaves, block sign-in and reset their password that same day, then reassign or remove their mailbox once their files are backed up.
Review the vendor and partner access list every six months and remove anyone you no longer work with.
google: In your checklist, note that access is cut in admin.google.com under Directory, then Users: select the person and choose 'Suspend user'.
From the same page, reset their password and remove them from Google Groups; use the data transfer tool if you need to move their Drive files first.
Add every outside vendor or IT provider with an admin role (Account, then Admin roles) to the list with a contact name.
When someone leaves, suspend the account that same day, then delete it once their files and email are transferred or backed up.
Review the vendor and admin role list every six months and remove anyone you no longer work with.

title: Set up a company password manager
whatToDo: Give staff a password manager so every account gets its own strong password without anyone needing to remember them.
why: Reused and written-down passwords are how one breach turns into many. A password manager makes the safe option the easy option.
steps: Pick a business password manager (for example Bitwarden, 1Password, or Keeper). Business plans cost a few dollars per user per month.
Set it up for the owner and office manager first, and move the most important passwords in: banking, email admin, and accounting.
Invite the rest of the team and show them how to save and fill passwords in a 15-minute huddle.
Use shared folders for team logins instead of passing passwords around by text or sticky note.

title: Remove admin rights from everyday accounts
whatToDo: Make sure day-to-day computer accounts are standard users, with admin rights kept to one or two people.
why: If an everyday account is an admin, one bad click lets ransomware install itself and spread. Standard accounts contain the damage.
steps: On each Windows computer, open Settings, then Accounts, then Other users, and check which accounts are 'Administrator'.
Change everyday accounts to 'Standard user'.
Keep a separate admin account for the one or two people who install software, and use it only when needed.
If you use Microsoft 365 or Google admin roles, check that only one or two people hold the top admin role.

m365: On each Windows computer, open Settings, then Accounts, then Other users, and check which accounts are 'Administrator'. Change everyday accounts to 'Standard user'.
Keep a separate local admin account for the one or two people who install software, and use it only when needed.
Go to entra.microsoft.com, open Identity, then Roles & admins, then 'Global Administrator', and confirm only one or two trusted people are assigned.
Turn on Security defaults (Identity, then Overview, then Properties) so anyone with an admin role must use MFA.
google: On each Windows computer, open Settings, then Accounts, then Other users, and check which accounts are 'Administrator'. Change everyday accounts to 'Standard user'.
Keep a separate local admin account for the one or two people who install software, and use it only when needed.
Go to admin.google.com, open Account, then Admin roles, then 'Super Admin', and confirm only one or two trusted people are assigned.
Turn on 2-step verification enforcement for anyone holding an admin role (Security, then Authentication, then 2-step verification).

title: Adopt a call-back rule for any bank detail change
whatToDo: Never change a supplier's, carrier's, or grower's bank details without calling them at a number you already had on file, and require a second approval for large payments.
why: Fake 'we changed banks' emails are the most common way small businesses lose money to fraud. A quick phone call to a trusted number stops it, at no cost.
steps: Write the rule down in one sentence: 'We only change bank details after calling the company at a number we already had on file.'
Never use the phone number in the email asking for the change. Use your records, the contract, or their public website.
Set a dollar limit (for example $5,000) above which a second person must approve the payment.
Tell everyone who handles payments today, and post the rule next to the accounting computer.
If a request feels rushed or secretive, treat that as a warning sign and slow down.

title: Run a 30-minute fake email awareness session
whatToDo: Walk staff through real examples of fake emails and turn on an 'External sender' warning in email.
why: Most attacks start with an email. A short, practical session makes people much more likely to pause before clicking or paying.
steps: Book 30 minutes with office staff and dispatchers. Use the free Get Cyber Safe materials from the Government of Canada as a guide.
Show 3 or 4 real examples: a fake invoice, a fake 'boss' asking for gift cards, a fake load board login page.
Agree on one simple rule: if unsure, forward it to one named person before clicking or paying.
Turn on an 'External' banner for emails from outside the company in your email admin settings.
Repeat a short refresher every year and whenever a new person joins.

m365: Book 30 minutes with office staff and dispatchers. Use the free Get Cyber Safe materials from the Government of Canada as a guide.
Show 3 or 4 real examples: a fake invoice, a fake 'boss' asking for gift cards, a fake load board login page.
Agree on one simple rule: if unsure, forward it to one named person before clicking or paying.

Turn on the external sender tag: an admin runs 'Set-ExternalInOutlook -Enabled $true' in Exchange Online PowerShell, or adds a mail flow rule in the Exchange admin center that prepends '[EXTERNAL]' to outside emails.
Repeat a short refresher every year and whenever a new person joins.
google: Book 30 minutes with office staff and dispatchers. Use the free Get Cyber Safe materials from the Government of Canada as a guide.
Show 3 or 4 real examples: a fake invoice, a fake 'boss' asking for gift cards, a fake load board login page.
Agree on one simple rule: if unsure, forward it to one named person before clicking or paying.
In admin.google.com open Apps, then Google Workspace, then Gmail, then End User Access, and turn on 'Warn for external recipients'. Also check Safety settings for spoofing protection.
Repeat a short refresher every year and whenever a new person joins.

title: Turn on DMARC for your email domain
whatToDo: Publish SPF and DMARC records for your domain so other companies' email systems can block emails faking your name.
why: Without DMARC, anyone can send email that looks like it came from you, including fake invoices to your own customers. It is free to set up.
steps: Log in to wherever your domain is registered (for example GoDaddy, Namecheap, or your web host) and open the DNS settings.
Make sure you have an SPF record (a TXT record starting with 'v=spf1') that lists your email provider.
Add a TXT record named '_dmarc' with the value 'v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@yourdomain.ca' to start collecting reports.
After 2 to 4 weeks with no problems, change 'p=none' to 'p=quarantine', and later to 'p=reject'.
Run the domain check in this tool again to confirm it is working.

m365: Log in to wherever your domain is registered (for example GoDaddy, Namecheap, or your web host) and open the DNS settings.
Check you have an SPF TXT record: 'v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com -all'.
In the Microsoft Defender portal (security.microsoft.com), open Email authentication settings, then DKIM, and turn on DKIM signing for your domain.
Add a TXT record named '_dmarc' with the value 'v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@yourdomain.ca'. After 2 to 4 weeks with no problems, change to 'p=quarantine', then 'p=reject'.
Run the domain check in this tool again to confirm it is working.
google: Log in to wherever your domain is registered (for example GoDaddy, Namecheap, or Google Domains / Squarespace) and open the DNS settings.
Check you have an SPF TXT record: 'v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all'.
In admin.google.com open Apps, then Google Workspace, then Gmail, then Authenticate email, and turn on DKIM.
Add a TXT record named '_dmarc' with the value 'v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@yourdomain.ca'. After 2 to 4 weeks with no problems, change to 'p=quarantine', then 'p=reject'.
Run the domain check in this tool again to confirm it is working.

title: Turn on automatic updates and antivirus everywhere
whatToDo: Make sure every computer installs security updates on its own and has Microsoft Defender or another antivirus switched on.
why: Most ransomware uses holes that already have a fix. Automatic updates and built-in antivirus block the bulk of everyday attacks for free.
steps: On each Windows computer, open Settings, then Windows Update, and make sure updates are on and not paused. Set active hours so restarts happen overnight.
Open Windows Security and check that Virus and threat protection shows green.
Turn on automatic updates for web browsers and common apps like Adobe Reader and Office.
Replace any computer running Windows 10 or older that can no longer receive updates.
Put a reminder on the calendar to spot-check every computer once a month.

title: Set up automatic backups with one offline copy and test a restore
whatToDo: Back up important data automatically, keep one copy disconnected or separate from your network, and prove you can restore it.
why: Backups are what let you recover from ransomware without paying. But ransomware also hunts for backups it can reach, so one copy must be out of reach.
steps: List what you cannot lose: accounting files, dispatch and load records, driver logs, customer lists, and email.
Set up an automatic daily backup to a cloud backup service (for example Backblaze, Acronis, or your IT provider's service) that keeps older versions.
Keep a second copy that is offline or separate: a drive you unplug and take off-site each week, or a cloud backup with 'immutable' or locked copies.
Once a quarter, pick a file or folder and actually restore it to prove the backup works.
Write down where the backups are and how to restore them, and keep it with your incident plan.

m365: List what you cannot lose: accounting files, dispatch and load records, driver logs, customer lists, and email.
If you use SharePoint, OneDrive, or Exchange Online, turn on Microsoft 365 Backup (search 'Backup' in admin.microsoft.com) to keep restorable copies of your files and mailboxes.

Also keep a second, separate copy offline or with a third-party cloud backup service that supports 'immutable' or locked copies. The default recycle bin and version history are not enough on their own.
Once a quarter, restore a file or mailbox item to prove the backup works.
Write down where the backups are and how to restore them, and keep it with your incident plan.
google: List what you cannot lose: accounting files, dispatch and load records, driver logs, customer lists, and email.

If you use Google Drive or Gmail, turn on Google Vault (admin.google.com, then Apps, then Google Workspace, then Vault) so files and email can be retained and recovered through vault.google.com. Also check Drive's version history and trash retention.
Also keep a second, separate copy offline or with a third-party cloud backup service that supports 'immutable' or locked copies. Vault and Drive's built-in history are not enough on their own.
Once a quarter, restore a file or email to prove the backup works.
Write down where the backups are and how to restore them, and keep it with your incident plan.

title: Lock down remote access to the office
whatToDo: Replace any open remote desktop connection with a secure remote access tool that requires a phone code.
why: Remote desktop left open to the internet is one of the top ways ransomware gangs break in. Closing it removes a major door.
steps: Ask whoever set up your network (or your IT provider) whether any computer has remote desktop (RDP, port 3389) open to the internet.
Close those openings on the router or firewall.
Use a secure remote access option with a phone code instead: a business VPN, or a remote access service with two-step login turned on.
Keep a list of who is allowed to connect from outside, and remove people when they leave.

title: Turn off always-on vendor remote access to equipment
whatToDo: Switch off TeamViewer, AnyDesk, or similar tools on equipment computers, and only turn them on when the vendor actually needs to connect.
why: Always-on remote access is an open door to your refrigeration and equipment. If the vendor or their password is compromised, attackers can walk straight in.
steps: Walk around and find every computer or controller that runs TeamViewer, AnyDesk, or a similar remote tool, especially refrigeration and monitoring systems.
Set the tool so it does not start automatically, or uninstall it and reinstall only when needed.
Agree with each vendor: they call you first, you turn access on, and you turn it off when they are done.
Change the remote access password and turn on two-step login in the tool if it offers it.
Add each vendor to your vendor access list.

title: Separate equipment and guest Wi-Fi from office network
whatToDo: Put connected equipment and guest or driver Wi-Fi on their own networks, separate from office computers.
why: Separate networks stop a problem in one place from spreading everywhere. An infected office computer should not be able to reach your refrigeration controls.
steps: Draw a simple map of what is connected: office computers, equipment and sensors, cameras, and guest or driver Wi-Fi.
Ask your IT provider or router supplier to create separate networks (VLANs) for equipment and for guests. Many business routers can do this.
Turn on the guest network option on your Wi-Fi and give drivers and visitors that password only.
Test that equipment still reports properly and that guests cannot see office computers.

title: Change default passwords on routers, cameras, and equipment
whatToDo: Replace every factory password on routers, cameras, controllers, and sensors with a unique strong one.
why: Default passwords are published online, and automated tools scan the internet for devices still using them.
steps: List every networked device: routers, Wi-Fi access points, cameras and recorders, refrigeration controllers, sensors, and printers.
Log in to each one and change the admin password to a unique strong one. Store them in your password manager.
While you are there, check for a firmware update and install it.
If a device will not let you change its password, ask the vendor about a replacement or keep it off the internet.

title: Add breach notification to vendor contracts
whatToDo: Ask vendors with access to your systems to commit, in writing, to telling you quickly if they are breached.
why: If a trusted vendor is compromised, you need to know fast so you can cut off their access before attackers use it against you.
steps: Start with your most important vendors: IT provider, refrigeration or equipment vendor, TMS or dispatch software, and payroll.
Send each a short request to add a clause saying they will notify you within 72 hours of any security incident that could affect you.
Add the same clause to your standard template for new vendor contracts.
Record who agreed on your vendor access list.

title: Write a one-page "if we're compromised" plan
whatToDo: Write one page that says who to call and what to do first if you are hit by ransomware or payment fraud.
why: A plan does not stop attacks, but it makes every attack less damaging. In a crisis, the first few hours decide how bad it gets.
steps: List who to call: your IT provider, your bank's fraud line, your insurer, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (1-833-CYBER-88).
Write the first three steps for ransomware: unplug affected computers from the network, do not pay or respond, call your IT provider.
Write the first three steps for payment fraud: call your bank immediately to recall the payment, report to local police and the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, warn the affected partner.
Note how to tell your key customers if their shipments or data could be affected.
Print it and keep a copy somewhere that does not need a computer to reach.

title: Get a cyber insurance quote
whatToDo: Ask your broker for a cyber insurance quote that covers ransomware, payment fraud, and incident response help.
why: Insurance helps cover recovery costs and usually includes expert help on the day. Many insurers also give discounts for the fixes on this list.
steps: Call your current business insurance broker and ask about cyber coverage.
Ask specifically whether it covers ransomware, funds transfer fraud (social engineering), and business interruption.
Have the answers from this check-up ready. Insurers will ask about two-step login, backups, and training.
Compare at least two quotes and check the incident response hotline is included.

title: Lock down load changes: call back and get a second OK
whatToDo: Any change to a pickup or delivery address is confirmed by calling the broker or shipper at a number you already had, and a second person OKs it before the driver is told.
why: Load theft by email works because one busy person can reroute a truck on the strength of a single message. A call to a known number and a second pair of eyes stops it, and it costs nothing.
steps: Write the rule down in one sentence: 'No pickup or delivery change goes to a driver until we've called the broker or shipper back on a number we already had, and a second person has OK'd it.'
Never use the phone number or link in the email asking for the change. Use the rate confirmation, your TMS, or the company's public website.
Pick who can give the second OK on each shift (for example, the dispatch lead or the owner) and make sure one of them is always reachable.
Watch for pressure: last-minute changes, a new consignee, 'urgent' wording, or a slightly different email address. Treat these as reasons to slow down.
Tell every dispatcher today, post the rule by the dispatch desk, and log each change with who called and who approved.

title: Replace or wall off computers that no longer get updates
whatToDo: Find every computer on an operating system that no longer gets security updates, replace it, or take it off the network until you can.
why: An unsupported computer keeps every security hole found after its last update, and attackers scan for exactly those. One old PC on the office network can be the way into everything else.
steps: List every computer, including PCs that run refrigeration, grain, or plant equipment. On Windows, open Settings, then System, then About to see the version. On a Mac, open the Apple menu, then About This Mac.
Flag anything on Windows 10 or older, or on a macOS version Apple no longer updates (Apple generally updates the three newest versions).
Replace office computers first. Windows 11 needs newer hardware, so many older PCs have to be replaced rather than upgraded.

For a PC that runs equipment and can't be replaced yet, ask the equipment vendor for a supported version. In the meantime, move it to a separate network with no internet access and never use it for email or browsing.
If you need more time, Microsoft sells Extended Security Updates for Windows 10 to businesses as a stopgap. Treat it as a deadline, not a fix.

title: Encrypt laptops and use only company USB drives
whatToDo: Turn on the encryption built into Windows and macOS on every laptop, and keep business files on company-owned, encrypted USB drives only.
why: Lost and stolen laptops and USB drives are the most common way small businesses leak customer and banking data. With encryption on, a lost device is a hardware cost, not a data breach.
steps: On each Windows laptop, open Settings and search for 'Device encryption' or 'BitLocker', and turn it on. It is included with Windows 11 Pro and on most newer laptops.
Save the recovery key somewhere other than the laptop. If the laptop signs in with a work Microsoft account, the key is saved to that account automatically; otherwise print it and lock it away.
On each Mac, open System Settings, then Privacy & Security, then FileVault, and choose Turn On.
Buy a few company USB drives and label them. On Windows Pro, right-click each drive and choose 'Turn on BitLocker' (BitLocker To Go) and set a password.
Tell staff that personal USB drives are not for business files, and wipe or physically destroy old drives before throwing them out.

title: Turn on sign-in alerts and name someone to check them
whatToDo: Send alerts about suspicious sign-ins and new email forwarding rules to a named person, block automatic forwarding outside the company, and agree what to do when an alert arrives.
why: Most payment and load fraud starts with a stolen email password, and criminals often watch a mailbox for weeks first. An alert that someone actually reads turns weeks into hours.
steps: Pick who receives security alerts (the owner or office manager, plus your IT company if you have one) and a backup for when they are away.
In your email provider's admin settings, turn on alerts for suspicious sign-ins and for new forwarding rules, and send them to that person.
Turn off automatic forwarding of email to addresses outside the company.
When an alert arrives, phone the person it is about (don't email them). If it wasn't them, reset their password, sign them out everywhere, and check their mailbox rules.

m365: Go to security.microsoft.com and sign in with your Microsoft 365 admin account.

Open Email & collaboration, then Policies & rules, then Alert policy. Check that the built-in alerts 'Creation of forwarding/redirect rule', 'Suspicious email forwarding activity', and 'User restricted from sending email' are on, and add your named person as a recipient on each.
Still under Policies & rules, open Threat policies, then Anti-spam, and edit the outbound spam filter policy. Set 'Automatic forwarding rules' to Off.

When an alert arrives, phone the person it is about. If it wasn't them, reset their password, choose 'Sign out of all sessions' on their account in the Microsoft 365 admin center, and delete any inbox rules they didn't create.
google: Go to admin.google.com and sign in with your Google Workspace admin account.
Open Rules. Edit the system-defined 'Suspicious login' and 'Leaked password' rules and turn on email notifications to your named person.
Open Apps, then Google Workspace, then Gmail, then End User Access. Under Automatic forwarding, uncheck 'Allow users to automatically forward incoming email to another address'.
Check Security, then Alert center once a week. When an alert arrives, phone the person it is about. If it wasn't them, reset their password and sign them out of all sessions from their user page.

title: Verify every new carrier before you tender a load
whatToDo: Before a load goes to a carrier you haven't used, check their registration and call them on a number from the official record, not the one they gave you.
why: Fake and hijacked carrier identities let criminals book a load, pick it up, and disappear. A registration check and one phone call to a number you found yourself stops most of them.
steps: Write the rule down in one sentence: 'No load goes to a new carrier until we've checked their registration and called them on a number we looked up ourselves.'

Check registration: for Canadian carriers, their National Safety Code (NSC) number with the provincial registry; for US carriers, their USDOT and MC numbers on the FMCSA SAFER website. Confirm the name, address, and how long they've held authority.
Call the phone number on the official record or the carrier's long-standing website, not the one in the email or load board message, and confirm they really booked this load.
Treat these as red flags: brand-new authority, a free email address, contact details that don't match the registration, pressure to move fast, or a request to pay a different company.
Keep a list of vetted carriers so repeat loads don't need the full check, and check again whenever a carrier's contact or payment details change.
